title: ThreadPool internals and thread starvation
description: Explore how the .NET ThreadPool manages worker threads, how it grows under load, and what thread starvation looks like in production applications.

data.text: Every time you call `Task.Run` or use `async`/`await` under the hood, the .NET ThreadPool is involved. Understanding how it works helps you avoid performance surprises in high-traffic applications.

The ThreadPool is a shared pool of worker threads maintained by the .NET runtime. Instead of creating a new thread for every small task, the runtime reuses existing threads. This reduces the overhead of thread creation and keeps memory usage predictable.

When you queue a work item, the ThreadPool assigns it to an available worker thread. If all threads are busy, the work waits in a queue until a thread becomes free. For most applications, this works seamlessly. Problems appear when the demand for threads exceeds the supply.

data.title: ThreadPool vs manual thread creation

data.text: The ThreadPool does not start with hundreds of threads. It starts small and adds threads when the queue grows. This process, called *hill climbing*, tries to find the right number of threads for the workload.

items: **Phase 1** — The ThreadPool starts with a small number of threads (typically one per CPU core).
**Phase 2** — If the queue stays busy, the ThreadPool injects new threads at a measured rate, usually one every 500 milliseconds.
**Phase 3** — If threads go idle, the ThreadPool slowly removes them to free resources.

data.title: Thread injection is not instant
data.text: The ThreadPool adds new threads gradually. If your application suddenly receives a burst of requests, threads may not appear fast enough. Requests pile up in the queue, latency spikes, and users experience slowdowns.

Thread starvation happens when all ThreadPool threads are busy and new work cannot make progress. In web applications, this often means HTTP requests stall because no thread is available to process them.

A common cause is *sync-over-async*: blocking on an async operation with `.Result` or `.Wait()`. The blocked thread sits idle while the async operation completes, yet the ThreadPool cannot reuse it for other work. Over time, this exhausts the pool.

data.title: Thread starvation caused by sync-over-async
Key takeaways
points: The ThreadPool reuses threads to avoid the cost of creating new ones.
Hill climbing adjusts thread count based on queue depth.
Thread starvation occurs when all threads are busy and new work waits.
Sync-over-async is a leading cause of starvation in production.
